notable_claims: At Wilfred Laurier University, newsgroups were banned based on the personal views of the Director of Computer Services.
Proposed netnews policies suggest that university library standards for intellectual freedom should apply to network material.
The Hatch Act is claimed not to forbid federal employees from expressing political opinions or engaging in general politics.
classification.summary: This digest summarizes several issues regarding academic computer freedom, including the banning of alt.sex newsgroups at Wilfred Laurier University and discussions on sexual harassment prevention. It provides model policy nominations for prohibitions, netnews standards, due process, and student participation in institutional policy. Additionally, it addresses the impact of the Hatch Act on the political expression of federal employees.
classification.title: Abstract of CAF-News 02.53

notable_claims: Seven newsgroups were banned at Wilfrid Laurier University due to offensive content.
The university president made the ban decision based on output from alt.sex groups.
University of Manitoba and Simon Fraser University also opted to ban these newsgroups.
University of Waterloo reinstated access to the alt.sex hierarchy after a previous ban.
classification.summary: Wilfrid Laurier University banned several newsgroups, specifically those in the alt.sex hierarchy, after administration deemed the content offensive. The decision was made by the university president following reports from computing services. Other Canadian institutions like the University of Manitoba and Simon Fraser University reportedly implemented similar bans, while the University of Waterloo maintained access.
classification.title: Newsgroups are banned

notable_claims: The author claims that the 'distinct society' guarantees in the proposed package could aggravate language right restrictions.
classification.summary: Mitch Pravatiner responds to a post by Hans Johnsen regarding constitutional amendments in Canada. The author argues that proposed language rights guarantees are insufficient due to existing escape clauses and the impact of Bill 101 in Quebec.
classification.title: Canadian Referendum and Language Rights

notable_claims: Harassment is determined by whether behavior is unwelcome, not by a priori lists of forbidden actions.
Technical restrictions like banning personal email or filtering words are ineffective and unnecessary for preventing harassment.
Computers are tools used by people to harass; the technology itself is not the source of the harassment.
classification.summary: Joseph A. Watters responds to a discussion on how to prevent sexual harassment within computer systems and academic environments. He argues that harassment is defined by whether behavior is 'unwelcome' rather than by specific prohibited acts, suggesting that draconian technical restrictions or lists of forbidden words are unnecessary. He asserts that computers are merely tools for communication and that existing disciplinary and legal frameworks should handle behavioral issues.
classification.title: Article 3--Re: Preventing Sexual Harassment?

notable_claims: The EFF house rules are suggested as a suitable model for academic site policies.
EFF system administrators commit to not reading mail or non-world-readable files unless absolutely necessary for their duties.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie proposes the Electronic Frontier Foundation's (EFF) house rules as a model for academic computer policies, emphasizing clear prohibitions and privacy protections. The post includes the EFF's 11-point policy regarding system access, security reporting, and administrator conduct. It also provides pointers to archives of various university computer policies hosted by the EFF, Widener University, and the University of New Mexico.
classification.title: Article 4--Best academic policy: prohibitions

notable_claims: Network news systems should be subject to the same standards of intellectual and academic freedom as university libraries.
Communications originating from campus to the network should be free of censorship or prior restraint.
Administrative restrictions on network access should only occur after consultation with faculty bodies.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie nominates the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee's network news policy as a model for academic freedom. The policy argues that Usenet access should be treated with the same intellectual freedom standards as university libraries and traditional publications. It specifically mandates that any administrative restrictions on network access must involve consultation with faculty governance bodies.
classification.title: Best academic policy: Netnews

notable_claims: Integrating computer ethics violations into general student and faculty handbooks provides a better model for due process than standalone policies.
The Iowa State University policy prohibits the use of university facilities for private monetary gain, political messages, or commercial nature.
classification.summary: Carl M. Kadie nominates Iowa State University's computer ethics policy as a model for due process because it integrates computer violations into existing university-wide disciplinary handbooks. The post includes the full text of ISU's policy and provides pointers to EFF and Widener archives of academic computer policies. Kadie notes that while the due process is strong, the policy's protections for privacy and free expression are lacking.
classification.title: Article 6--Best academic policy: due process

notable_claims: Ideal academic policies should be developed with the broadest possible participation of the academic community.
Students should be free to express views on institutional policy and have defined means to participate in its formulation.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie seeks nominations for the best model of student and faculty participation in creating academic computer policies. He cites a Joint Statement on Rights and Freedoms of Students as an ideal framework, emphasizing that students should have defined means to participate in institutional policy formulation. The post also provides access details for the Electronic Frontier Foundation's archive of school computer policies and critiques.
classification.title: Article 7--Best academic policy: participation

notable_claims: The Hatch Act does not apply to students or grantees.
ISU's computer speech restriction prohibiting political purposes is likely overly broad.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie critiques a computer speech restriction at Iowa State University (ISU) that forbids the use of facilities for political purposes. He argues that the justification based on the Hatch Act is legally flawed as it applies to federal employees rather than students or grantees. Kadie suggests the ISU policy is overly broad and contrasts it with evolving university rules against censorship.
classification.title: Prohibiting "political" expression

notable_claims: The Hatch Act applies only to Federal employees, not recipients of federal grants or government contractors.
The Hatch Act does not forbid federal employees from expressing political opinions.
There are no federal laws imposing restrictions on political expression via campus computers.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding university policies that prohibit the use of campus computers for political expression. Joe Buck argues against the claim that the Hatch Act justifies such restrictions, asserting that federal law does not forbid political expression on campus computers.
classification.title: Prohibiting "political" expression
